faq.a: Heavy manual labor, poor ergonomics and untreated infections increase mechanical and infectious causes.
faq.q: Why is low back pain so common in low‑resource settings?

faq.a: Fracture follows trauma with acute pain and height loss; discitis presents with fever, elevated ESR and gradual pain.
faq.q: What distinguishes a compression fracture from discitis?

faq.a: Progressive neurological deficit, spinal instability, or failure of conservative therapy after 6‑8 weeks.
faq.q: When is surgery indicated for lumbar pathology?

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer presents with sudden lumbar pain after lifting a sack – what is your immediate bedside assessment and why? — Assess for fracture (palpate spinous processes, check for height loss, neuro exam) to rule out instability before mobilising.
How does the orientation of lumbar facet joints influence the pattern of injury? — Sagittal orientation permits flexion/extension but limits rotation, making shear injuries common in falls.

A patient with HIV and chronic back pain has an ESR of 90 mm/h; what diagnosis should be high on your list and what test confirms it? — Suspect tuberculous spondylitis; MRI of the spine is the confirmatory test.

Explain why a positive straight‑leg raise differentiates disc herniation from muscular strain. — Raises tension on the sciatic nerve, reproducing radicular pain, which is absent in pure muscle strain.
What are the red‑flag features that mandate urgent imaging in low‑back pain? — Trauma, neurological deficit, fever, weight loss, immunosuppression, and progressive deformity.

Describe the steps to perform a Schober test and its clinical relevance. — Mark 10 cm above and 5 cm below the lumbosacral junction, ask patient to flex; increase < 5 cm suggests limited lumbar flexion.

In a setting without MRI, how would you evaluate a suspected epidural abscess? — Use contrast‑enhanced CT if available; otherwise, rely on clinical signs (fever, back pain, neurological deficit) and start empiric antibiotics.

Why are high‑dose NSAIDs avoided in patients with chronic kidney disease presenting with back pain? — They can worsen renal function and cause gastrointestinal bleeding; consider acetaminophen or opioid sparingly.
ai.title: Lumbar Spine Anatomy
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The lumbar spine provides support, mobility and protects the spinal cord cauda equina. Understanding its bony, ligamentous and neurovascular relationships guides diagnosis of low‑back pain in low‑resource settings.

b: Largest vertebral bodies in the spine
No foramina in the vertebral arch
Intervertebral discs act as shock absorbers
sections.p: The lumbar region consists of five vertebrae (L1‑L5) that bear most of the body weight and allow flexion, extension and limited rotation.

b: Body height ≈ 2‑3 cm, width ≈ 4‑5 cm
Pedicles project posteriorly to form the canal
Facet joints oriented sagittally, permitting flexion/extension
sections.p: Each lumbar vertebra has a thick body, a short spinous process, long transverse processes and robust laminae forming the vertebral canal.

b: Aorta bifurcates at L4
Kidneys lie at L1‑L3
Psoas major attaches to transverse processes
sections.p: Anteriorly the lumbar spine lies against the abdominal aorta, inferior vena cava and retroperitoneal organs; posteriorly it is covered by the erector spinae muscles.

b: Anterior spinal artery receives contributions at each level
Veins form a valveless plexus that drains to the azygos system
sections.p: Segmental lumbar arteries arise from the abdominal aorta and supply the vertebral bodies, discs and posterior elements via the spinal branches.

b: Femoral nerve (L2‑L4) supplies anterior thigh
Obturator nerve (L2‑L4) supplies medial thigh
Lumbosacral trunk (L4‑L5) joins sacral plexus
sections.p: The lumbar spinal nerves exit below each vertebra, forming the lumbar plexus (L1‑L4) and contributing to the sacral plexus.

b: Absorbs compressive forces via discs
Stabilises trunk during lifting
Protects cauda equina and spinal nerves
sections.p: Provides axial support, transmits load from the thorax to the pelvis, and permits flexion, extension and limited rotation essential for daily activities.

b: Compression fracture: sudden back pain after fall, height loss
Disc herniation: radicular pain, positive straight‑leg raise
Pott disease: chronic back pain, gibbus deformity, night sweats
sections.p: Low‑back pain is common; pathology may involve vertebral fractures, disc degeneration, infection or tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease).

t.b: Detects fractures, alignment, gross disc space loss; if unavailable, use clinical assessment and treat as fracture until proven otherwise
Identifies disc herniation, epidural abscess, TB; if not available, rely on CT or bedside ultrasound for fluid collections
Elevated in infection/TB; normal does not exclude mechanical causes

b: Schober test < 5 cm indicates limited flexion
Positive straight‑leg raise at 30‑70° suggests nerve root irritation
Weak ankle dorsiflexion points to L4‑L5 radiculopathy
sections.p: Key bedside maneuvers: inspection for deformity, palpation of spinous processes, lumbar flexion (Schober test), straight‑leg raise, and neuro‑vascular assessment of lower limbs.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe back pain with fever or night sweats
